title: P0 Ephemeral Concurrency Stall — Hosted API Review
summary: A sudden traffic pattern of thousands of short, high-QPS requests caused the hosted API dispatcher to create a large number of ephemeral execution contexts that saturated ephemeral worker slots and held a routing mutex. The mutex contention prevented the normal batching/stride-aggregation path from serving requests, producing widespread request stalls and streaming 5xx responses. An automated kill-switch (circuit breaker) misfired during recovery which amplified error rates and delayed full service restoration.
impact: Approximately 37% of hosted-api requests experienced tail latency > 5s or 5xx responses for a 49-minute window. Streaming responses failed mid-stream for many long-running client sessions. Several production customers reported degraded UX and we paged on-call; revenue impact is estimated as low-to-medium but several high-tier customers were affected and SLO breaches occurred for the Hosted API route. Internal metrics: peak concurrent ephemeral contexts hit 18k (baseline 2.2k), worker saturation reached 96% on inference cluster pool A.
timeline:
09:11:58Z — Normal traffic; routine deploy of lightweight config change scheduled but not yet promoted.
09:12:04Z — First signs of increased short-prompt traffic from a single customer region (APAC gateway) (Alert: short-prompt-qps > 4x baseline).
09:12:22Z — Dispatcher starts creating many ephemeral execution contexts to avoid per-request cold starts (design behavior for low-latency).
09:12:47Z — Global routing mutex acquisition latency begins to climb; internal metric 'route.acquire.ms' exceeds 500ms.
09:13:05Z — Worker pool A reports queue length growth; autoscaler not triggered because ephemeral contexts bypassed autoscale metric.
09:14:12Z — First user-facing 5xx spike; streaming sessions observe 'stream closed' errors.
09:15:00Z — SRE on-call paged; initial hypothesis: downstream hardware issue.
09:17:30Z — Team identifies high mutex contention in dispatcher leading to request serialization.
09:19:10Z — On-call triggers mitigation: reduce ephemeral context creation rate (dynamic config toggle). Toggle partially applied but one service instance had stale config and continued creating contexts.
09:25:40Z — Circuit breaker (kill-switch) threshold for one autoscale shard tripped and flipped to 'protect' state; traffic routed to fallback model variant that was incompatible with streaming path, causing additional 5xx.
09:31:00Z — Rollback of last config deploy initiated to ensure consistent config; propagation completed by 09:35:00Z.
09:36:20Z — Dynamic toggle correctly applied across all instances; ephemeral context creation rate limited; dispatcher mutex contention decreases.
09:40:12Z — Circuit breaker reset manually; fallback model traffic gracefully drained.
09:46:50Z — Metrics show worker utilization returning to normal.
10:01:00Z — Incident declared resolved (no elevated error rates for 15m); postmortem created and owners assigned for follow-ups.
root_cause: A combination of an unusual traffic pattern (sudden high-QPS of short prompts) and a runtime behavior that eagerly spawned ephemeral execution contexts to avoid cold starts. This created extreme mutex contention in the dispatcher routing path. The autoscaler did not react because ephemeral contexts were not accounted for in autoscale signals. During the recovery, an automated circuit-breaker engaged and routed traffic to a fallback path that did not support streaming, producing additional 5xx and prolonging recovery. A config propagation gap (one instance with stale config) meant the initial mitigation was partially effective until a full rollback and manual correction were performed.
contributing_factors:
1) Design choice: ephemeral execution contexts spawn aggressively for short prompts to minimize P99 latency but lack a global admission-cap.
2) Observability gap: ephemeral context creation metric was not part of autoscaling nor included on main incident dashboards.
3) Safeguard misconfiguration: circuit breaker fallback path didn't support streaming and had an incompatibility matrix not covered by automated tests.
4) Deployment/config propagation: a small percentage of instances kept stale config and ignored the dynamic limiter.
5) Runbook gap: the 'dispatcher mutex' symptom was not documented in runbooks, leading to slower initial diagnosis.
detection: Detected by synthetic short-prompt latency alert and increased 5xx error rate on hosted-api/streaming route. Pager routed to SRE on-call. Early Slack thread: #sre-oncall, timestamped alerts included aggregated 'route.acquire.ms' and 'hosted-api.5xx_rate'. Detection-to-page was ~3 minutes.
mitigation_and_recovery:
Immediate mitigations applied:
- Dynamic limiter toggle to cap ephemeral context creation rate (partial at 09:19; full at 09:36).
- Manual rollback of the config change to eliminate propagation discrepancies (09:31–09:35).
- Manual reset of faulty circuit breaker to allow normal routing and streaming support (09:40).
- Rate-limited ingress for the offending region for 20 minutes to reduce load while cluster recovered.
Recovery steps:
- Drain and restart a subset of dispatcher workers to clear stuck mutex state (completed 09:44).
- Verify streaming endpoints by running end-to-end streaming health checks to key customers.
- Monitor metrics for 30m post-recovery before closing incident.

runbook_changes:
- Add new page 'Dispatcher mutex contention' with fast triage checklist and metrics to watch (route.acquire.ms, ephemeral_context_count, worker.queue_len).
- Add a 'flip-mode' test to the circuit-breaker CI job that validates fallback supports streaming.
- Document dynamic limiter toggle name and safe values; include a rollback checklist.
- Include ephemeral_context_count as an autoscale signal and add visible threshold alert (warning at 70% of capacity).
lessons_learned:
1) Optimizations that reduce latency at P99 (ephemeral contexts) can create new systemic admission problems at scale — always consider global admission limits.
2) Observability and autoscaling must include any 'hidden' resource consumers (ephemeral contexts, ephemeral caches).
3) Automated protect mechanisms (circuit-breakers) need compatibility checks for important features (streaming).
4) Small config propagation failures during incidents materially slow mitigation — ensure deploy tooling has canary verification.
5) Runbooks should prioritize symptoms (mutex contention) over internal terms so triage is faster for on-call responders.
